Belarus General Strike Disrupts Industry and Services; Major Miner Reports Production Halt

MINSK, June 14—A nationwide general strike in Belarus entered its second day on Friday, disrupting key sectors including mining, manufacturing, transport, and logistics. Belorusskaya Gorno Metallurgicheskaya Kompaniya OAO, one of the country’s largest mining and metallurgical firms, confirmed it had suspended production at its main facility in Gomel region due to worker walkouts.

The strike, organized by a coalition of independent unions, is the largest cross-sector industrial action in Belarus in over a decade. The Belarusian Confederation of Labor estimated that tens of thousands of workers from public transport operators, chemical plants, and food processing companies have joined the action, demanding higher wages and protest against recent labor law changes. According to union representatives, participation remains high, with more workers joining since Thursday’s kickoff.

“Production lines are at a standstill. Only essential personnel are on site to ensure safety,” said Andrei Kovalenko, spokesperson for Belorusskaya Gorno Metallurgicheskaya Kompaniya OAO. “Every hour of downtime is a significant loss for the company and the region.”

Other major employers, such as the state rail operator and Smolensk Agroexport, also reported severe disruption, with freight services and agricultural shipments delayed or suspended. The Belarus Chamber of Commerce estimated that economic losses from the strike could exceed $40 million if disruptions persist through the weekend.

Government officials have called for negotiations but warned that unauthorized protests could face legal consequences. “We urge all parties to return to dialogue. The government is ready to address concerns within the framework of the law,” said Deputy Economy Minister Irina Shestakova in a televised address.

Analysts say the strike’s duration will be critical. “If the action continues into next week, the impact on exports and industrial supply chains could be substantial,” said Pavel Melnikov, an economist at the Minsk Policy Center. “Belarus is highly dependent on industrial output, so prolonged disruption carries significant economic risks.”

As of Friday afternoon, strike organizers vowed to continue until their demands are met.
